papers.title: REM Sleep Iota Oscillations Across the Lifespan
papers.abstract: Iota oscillations are a newly discovered marker of wakefulness and rapid eye movement (REM) sleep. So far, iota in REM sleep has only been reported in the surface electroencephalography (EEG) of a small sample of young adults and in intracranial recordings of epileptic patients. Here, we investigated the presence of these oscillations in a large dataset (N=937) of high-density sleep EEG recordings from individuals 7 to 70 years old. We found that iota spectral peaks during REM sleep were between 25 and 40 Hz, slightly faster than in wake (25-35 Hz). Iota power was significantly associated with REM sleep architecture, increasing with both REM duration and across progressive sleep cycles. Iota peaks were observed in individuals of all ages, although the prevalence decreased gradually with age, from 88% in children to 44% in older adults. Most iota spectral peak properties (frequency, amplitude, timing, topography) likewise shifted with age. The most striking effect, however, was in bandwidth, such that children had narrow iota peaks, older adults had broad iota peaks, and 20-30 year olds could have either. It remains unclear whether narrowband and broadband iota are functionally equivalent. On shorter time scales (< 1 year), iota properties remained stable across measurements. Analyses of a separate dataset of monozygotic and dizygotic twins revealed high heritability of all iota peak properties except bandwidth. Overall, these results establish iota as a genetically determined trait-like marker of REM sleep with unique age-related changes. Iota oscillations open new avenues to investigate the interaction between sleep, genetics, development, and aging.

papers.title: Sleep Stage Classification Across Heterogeneous EEG/EOG Channels with Multi-channel Differential Transformer.
papers.abstract: Classification of sleep stages is essential for assessing sleep quality and diagnosing sleep disorders. However, manual inspection of EEG characteristics for each stage is time-consuming and prone to human error. Although machine learning and deep learning methods have been actively developed, they continue to face challenges arising from the non-stationarity and variability of electroencephalography (EEG) and electrooculography (EOG) signals across diverse clinical configurations, often resulting in poor generalization. In this work, we propose SleepDIFFormer, a multi-channel differential transformer framework for heterogeneous EEG-EOG representation learning. SleepDIFFormer is trained across multiple sleep staging datasets, each treated as a source domain, with the goal of generalizing to unseen target domains. Specifically, it employs a Multi-channel Differential Transformer Architecture (MDTA) designed to process raw EEG and EOG signals while incorporating cross-domain alignment. Our approach mitigates spatial and temporal attention noise and learns a domain-invariant EEG-EOG representation through feature distribution alignment across datasets, thereby enhancing generalization to new domains. Empirically, we evaluated SleepDIFFormer on five diverse sleep staging datasets under domain generalization settings and benchmarked it against existing approaches, achieving superior performance. Furthermore, comprehensive ablation analyses and interpretation of the differential attention weights demonstrated their relevance to learning discriminative sleep EEG representations. These findings support the development of more generalizable approaches to automated sleep-stage classification. Our source code and checkpoint are made publicly available at https://github.com/Ben1001409/SleepDIFFormer.

ai.reason: Directly targets generalizable sleep staging across heterogeneous EEG/EOG channels with domain alignment; core relevance, though transformer training may be more GPU-dependent than desired.
ai.summary: Proposed SleepDIFFormer, a multi-channel differential transformer framework using cross-domain alignment for domain-generalizable sleep stage classification from raw heterogeneous EEG/EOG, and reported superior performance versus existing approaches across five sleep staging datasets under domain generalization settings.

papers.title: Enhancing cortical electrophysiological signatures of sleep overrides ER stress responses in sleep-deprived mice
papers.abstract: Sleep deprivation (SD) triggers characteristic changes in the cortical electroencephalogram (EEG) during waking and sleep, as well as upregulating molecular signatures of neuronal activity, synaptic plasticity, and endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress. This includes the induction of the unfolded protein response (UPR), the primary marker and adaptive mechanism of ER stress. Yet how cortical neuronal activity during SD contributes to the induction of these molecular signatures remains unknown. Here we investigate whether manipulating cortical activity during SD with a physiological stimulation paradigm (flickering light stimulation, FLS) affects the induction of the UPR. As expected, SD alone upregulated activity-dependent and UPR-related genes in cortex and led to increased EEG slow-wave activity (SWA) during subsequent NREM sleep, an electrophysiological signature of sleep need. Delivering FLS during SD, however, prevented the upregulation of activity- and UPR-related genes while inducing an additional increase in SWA during subsequent sleep. Further analysis of neuronal firing revealed that FLS induced brief neuronal silent (OFF) periods in awake animals during stimulation, thereby shifting cortical activity towards a brain state resembling sleep. These findings suggest that physiological manipulation of cortical activity during waking is sufficient to dissociate molecular signatures of ER stress from electrophysiological markers of sleep pressure. We propose that global sleep wake history and cortical network dynamics differentially regulate activity-dependent transcription and the accumulation of sleep pressure.

papers.title: Circadian and Sleep-Wake Modulation of EEG Functional Connectivity Across Brain States and Its Associations With Cognition in Humans.
papers.abstract: Sleep and circadian rhythms both influence human brain function, but their distinct contributions to large-scale network organization remain unclear. We quantified the effect of brain state (wake, NREM, REM), sleep-wake history, and circadian phase on functional connectivity using over 1,200 hours of artifact-free EEG recorded during a 10-day forced-desynchrony protocol. We derived principal components of functional connectivity and found that both sleep-wake history and circadian phase significantly modulated functional connectivity, with sleep-wake history exerting a broader influence. Complementary cosinor analyses further demonstrated circadian rhythmicity in several NREM and REM connectivity measures. Across sleep, global connectivity increased progressively during NREM sleep, particularly in the delta and sigma bands, but declined during REM sleep. During controlled resting wakefulness, increasing time awake was associated with higher global alpha-band connectivity, which was associated with poorer concurrent cognitive performance. Connectivity during NREM sleep was also associated with subsequent cognitive performance, with lower global theta and, to a lesser extent, higher sigma connectivity linked to better performance. REM connectivity was not associated with these cognitive measures. Together, these findings reveal opposing NREM and REM trajectories in large-scale EEG functional connectivity and show that these brain-state-specific network dynamics are shaped by both sleep-wake history and circadian phase and are associated with cognitive performance.

ai.summary: Using over 1,200 hours of artifact-free EEG from a 10-day forced-desynchrony protocol, the study showed that sleep-wake history and circadian phase both modulate EEG functional connectivity, with sleep-wake history having broader influence. Global connectivity increased across NREM sleep (especially delta and sigma bands) but declined during REM, and state-specific connectivity measures were associated with cognitive performance.

papers.title: Single-Lead EEG-based virtual reality motion sickness detection using interpretable feature selection.
papers.abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) is a key method for detecting virtual reality motion sickness (VRMS), but multi-lead recordings and high-dimensional features increase processing complexity, device cost, and user burden. This study proposes a SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP)-based single-lead modeling and feature-screening framework to reduce the number of EEG leads and feature dimensions for lightweight VRMS detection. Six classical deep-learning EEG decoding models were used to assess the contribution of each lead via SHAP values and identify the optimal single lead. Handcrafted features were then extracted and selected using a correlation-SHAP strategy, and XGBoost was adopted for final classification. FT11 showed competitive and relatively consistent performance across the evaluated models and was selected as the target lead after integrating SHAP-based lead importance, single-lead classification performance, frequency-band differences, and physiological relevance. Under the window-level tenfold cross-validation protocol used in this study, the proposed model achieved an accuracy of 87.53% ± 0.73% using seven selected features, which was 9.55 percentage points lower than the full-lead full-feature model and 0.69 percentage points lower than the single-lead full-feature model. These findings demonstrate an interpretable framework for identifying a compact single-lead and feature configuration for VRMS-related EEG discrimination. An additional post hoc LOSO test of the globally selected configuration showed limited performance on held-out participants. Because the lead, classifier, and feature configuration had been selected globally before LOSO testing, these results should not be interpreted as a fully independent estimate of cross-subject generalization.

Under window-level tenfold cross-validation it achieved 87.53% ± 0.73% accuracy, with a post hoc LOSO test showing limited cross-subject generalization.

papers.title: Comparing re-referencing methods for human intracranial EEG
papers.abstract: Stereo-electroencephalography (SEEG) involves the implantation of depth electrodes in the brain to monitor epileptic seizures for surgical feasibility. As the electrodes advance into deeper limbic structures, the macro contacts distributed along the shaft record electrical activity from more lateral sites, while a bundled array of microwires simultaneously captures highly localised signals from the tip of the electrode. In a clinical setting these electrical signals are recorded relative to a reference signal, which may be sub-optimal for subsequent analyses that are unrelated to clinical objectives. Therefore, a secondary re-referencing operation is often undertaken to transform the signal in relation to a specific hypothesis. Despite a recent surge in SEEG studies, comparative studies on the much-understudied issue of re-referencing are sparse. Here, we analyse data collected from 16 human patients during an episodic memory task and comparatively apply a range of re-referencing methods to both macro contact and micro-wire data. We find that the choice of method changes the proportion of trials that survive artefact rejection, low frequency power, and the aperiodic background against which that power is read. In the hippocampal recordings, however, no method differed from any other in the size of a memory effect in power or spike-field coherence. This early transformative decision therefore bears on how the signal is described. We found no evidence that it changes the detectability of the behavioural effects tested here, and no method reversed the direction of a memory effect.

ai.reason: Systematic comparison of re-referencing choices affecting artifact rejection and power/aperiodic background; highly transferable to signal normalization across recording systems.
ai.summary: This study compared re-referencing methods on macro-contact and microwire SEEG data from 16 epilepsy patients performing an episodic memory task, finding that method choice altered artifact-rejection survival, low-frequency power, and aperiodic background. In hippocampal recordings, however, no method changed the magnitude or direction of the memory effect in power or spike-field coherence.

papers.title: Beyond Mean Pooling: Statistical Meta-Aggregation for Subject-Level EEG Classification in Parkinson's Disease
papers.abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) provides a non-invasive, temporally precise tool for studying neural alterations associated with Parkinson's disease (PD). When labels are defined at the subject level but inputs are epoch level, a key design choice is how epoch-wise predictions are aggregated to a single subject-level decision. Most prior work uses mean pooling, which assumes all epochs contribute equally and independently. This study proposes a statistical meta-aggregation strategy that represents each subject by 14 descriptors of the epoch-wise prediction distribution, including measures of central tendency, dispersion, shape, and high-confidence concentration. Using a self-supervised contrastive encoder trained on task-evoked EEG from the Simon conflict task, and a sample of 90 subjects including 57 PD and 33 control, this work evaluates the proposed framework under subject-wise five-fold cross-validation. Replacing mean pooling with statistical meta-aggregation lifts subject-level ROC-AUC from 0.655 to 0.872 for logistic regression and from 0.724 to 0.840 for support vector machines, without modifying the encoder or the classifier family. Averaging predictions across three independent self-supervised pretraining seeds yields competitive performance and improved balanced accuracy. These results suggest that, in this dataset, the way epoch-level predictions are summarized at the subject level has a substantial effect on final PD classification performance.

papers.title: Artefact-free EEG during temporal interference stimulation reveals phase-specific modulation of the human visual cortex
papers.abstract: Background: Temporal interference (TI) stimulation applies kHz electric fields whose envelope is modulated at a difference frequency ({Delta}f), allowing non-invasive deep-brain targeting. Measuring the neural response during stimulation with EEG is essential for establishing mechanisms and for closed-loop control. However, non-linearities in the recording chain mix the kHz carriers, producing an artefact at exactly {Delta}f. Objectives: To establish a method for recording EEG during TI without the {Delta}f artefact, and to test whether TI modulates neural activity at {Delta}f. Methods: A front-end analogue low-pass filter (7th order; 90 Hz cut-off; [≥]130 dB attenuation at 1 kHz) was bench-tested. In 22 healthy participants, residual artefact was assessed per recording with a two-stage detection pipeline in stimulation-only blocks. TI targeted the right primary visual cortex at 10 or 15.5 Hz, in-phase or anti-phase with multi-frequency photic stimulation (4.5, 10, 15.5 Hz), during a choice reaction time task. Results: The filter suppressed the {Delta}f artefact below the noise floor on a resistive load. In vivo, residual artefact was confirmed in two participants and could not be excluded in two more; all four were excluded from EEG analyses. Steady-state visual evoked potential (SSVEP) amplitude at 11, 14.5 and 15.5 Hz predicted faster responses. In-phase 15.5 Hz TI increased SSVEP amplitude at 14.5 and 15.5 Hz and shortened response times relative to both sham and anti-phase TI, which did not differ from sham. Conclusions: With front-end filtering and per-recording verification, EEG can measure TI neuromodulation during stimulation and at {Delta}f, revealing phase-specific modulation of visual entrainment linked to behaviour.

papers.title: EEG-Based Characterization of Cortical Dynamics during Graded Resistance Exercise.
papers.abstract: Understanding how brain activity varies during voluntary movement under different resistance conditions may provide insights into neural responses associated with physical demands and inform the development of neurorehabilitation strategies. In this study, we investigated changes in neural activity associated with increasing resistance levels during unilateral bicep curl movement. Ten healthy participants performed bicep curls under five resistance conditions while their cortical activity was recorded using electroencephalography (EEG). Movement-related cortical potentials (MRCPs), power spectral density (PSD) topographies, nonparametric spatiotemporal cluster-based permutation tests and linear mixed-effects models (LMMs) were used to characterize EEG differences across resistance conditions. Differences in MR-CPs and frequency-specific power spectral density (PSD) patterns were observed across resistance conditions, with significant spatiotemporal clusters identified during pre-movement, peak contraction, and movement execution phases. A Triplet Temporal Convolutional Network (TTCN) was also employed to learn latent representations from these EEG signals, and its discriminative capability was evaluated using a k-nearest neighbors (KNN) classifier. The learned embeddings showed separation between the resistance conditions, with classification errors occurring primarily between neighboring conditions. Using a within subject leave-one-trial-out (LOTO) evaluation strategy, the TTCN-KNN framework achieved accuracy of 97.2%. Furthermore, subject-independent evaluation were conducted using a leave-one-subject-out (LOSO) approach, achieving a maximum accuracy of 93.0%. These findings suggest that EEG signals contain discriminative information for distinguishing the resistance conditions in both within-subject and subject-independent settings, providing preliminary in sights for future EEG-based monitoring of motor effort and adaptive brain-machine interface applications.

papers.title: Delineating neural contributions to electroencephalogram-based speech decoding.
papers.abstract: Objective. Speech Brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) have emerged as a pivotal technology in facilitating communication for individuals with speech impairments. Utilizing electroencephalography (EEG) for noninvasive speech BCIs offers an accessible and affordable solution, potentially benefiting a broader audience. However, EEG-based speech decoding remains controversial especially for overt speech, due to difficulties in separating speech-related neural activities from myoelectric potential artifacts generated during articulation. Moreover, because paradigms for collecting covert speech data are inherently less scalable than those for overt speech, whether the neural dynamics underlying EEG-based decoding of overt speech are also present during covert speech remains an open and practically important question.Approach. Here we aim to delineate the extent of the neural contributions to EEG-based speech decoding, and the degree to which the underlying neural dynamics are shared across overt and covert speech, by employing Explainable AI techniques to a convolutional neural network predicting spoken words based on signals obtained by ultra-high-density (uhd)-EEG.Main results. We found that electrode-wise contributions to the decoding cannot be explained by their mutual information with electromyography (EMG). Furthermore, contributing periods of speech to EEG-based decoding are distinct from those to decoding solely relying on EMG. In contrast, there are significant overlaps in signal timings contributing to EEG-based decoding, regardless of vocal conditions such as overt or covert speech. Notably, the denoising process successfully enhanced the decoding contribution from electrodes within speech-related brain areas for all speech conditions.Significance. Altogether, our findings support the idea that, with appropriate preprocessing, EEG becomes a valuable tool for decoding spoken words based on underlying neural activities.&#xD.

Denoising enhanced contributions from speech-related brain areas, supporting EEG-based neural speech decoding after appropriate preprocessing.

papers.title: Bombadil: A Foundation Model for Plant Electrophysiology
papers.abstract: Living plants, like animals, use electrical signals to carry information about their physiological state across their body, from roots to branches. These signals can be recorded, as they are in animals, from a pair of differential extracellular electrodes inserted into signal-conducting tissue. While machine-learning models have been trained to predict specific plant stress states from these signals, each of these models has been trained for only a single task and none have been designed to transfer across tasks, species, or environments. These approaches do not allow easy scaling across the wide range of species and environments that are relevant to agriculture, forestry, and horticulture for both commercial and consumer plant care. Here we present Bombadil, a foundation model for plant electrophysiology, pretrained without labels on over 4 million hours of electrical signals recorded from 100 plant species in ten distinct environments, including laboratories, greenhouses, commercial orchards, and natural forests. In this way, Bombadil is able to learn the fundamental features of plant electrical signals across a wide array of species and environments. Then, from those same electrical signals, Bombadil tracks changes in seven physiological indicators of plant stress, even among species and stressors with no labels in training.

ai.reason: Large-scale extracellular electrophysiology foundation model transferable across species; conceptually interesting for cross-dataset generalization but not EEG/sleep specific.
ai.summary: Bombadil is a foundation model for plant electrophysiology pretrained without labels on over 4 million hours of electrical signals from 100 plant species across ten environments. It tracks changes in seven physiological indicators of plant stress, including in species and stressors with no labels in training.

papers.title: A feature-optimized EEG framework using multiscale entropy and metaheuristic optimization for cognitive analysis.
papers.abstract: Cognitive activity plays an important role by influencing working-memory, problem-solving, attention, response and decision making. EEG serves as a non-invasive approach to analyze neural activity associated with cognitive processing. The current study aims to identify the more contributing features to analyze the cognitive activity between sports and non-sports groups. The present study included 100 participants, consisting of 80 males and 20 females aged between 19 and 23 years. EEG signals were acquired and preprocessed using filtering methods to remove unwanted noise and artifacts. The four-entropy metrics dispersion entropy, permutation entropy, sample entropy, and fuzzy entropy were applied to the coarse-graining method across multiple temporal scales to analyze the complexity of EEG signals. To identify the most informative feature subsets and reduce redundancy, filter-based methods such as Mutual Information, Pearson Correlation, Minimum Redundancy Maximum Relevance and wrapper-based methods such as Genetic Algorithm and Particle Swarm Optimization were applied. Finally for differentiating the cognitive activity, five machine learning classifiers that include Support Vector Machine, Artificial Neural Network, K-nearest neighbor, Decision Tree and Random Forest were applied. Statistical methods such as T-test and Fleiss kappa were used to analyse the performance efficiency. Feature extraction phase yielded a total of 160 multiscale entropy features. The entire features when fed into both filter-based and wrapper-based methods, Genetic Algorithm based optimization yielded a minimal contributing feature subset with high nested cross-validated accuracy of 93.0 ± 2.7% with Support Vector Machine. This contributing feature subset was used as input for five different machine learning classifiers for differentiating the cognitive activity between both groups. The five classifiers demonstrated high cross-validated agreement on held-out subjects, with a mean Fleiss' kappa of 0.874 ± 0.051 (95% CI: 0.811-0.937), depicting a good inter-classifier agreement for classification of samples into sports and non-sports individuals. The study demonstrates that multiscale entropy features combined with metaheuristic-based feature optimization can effectively analyze the cognitive activity between sports and non-sports individuals. The proposed EEG framework provides a structured approach for real-time cognitive activity analysis using compact and informative entropy-based feature subsets.

ai.reason: Interpretable entropy-based feature extraction and optimization is somewhat relevant to lightweight EEG analysis, though applied to cognitive group comparison rather than sleep or transfer.
ai.summary: The study applied multiscale entropy features (dispersion, permutation, sample, fuzzy) with filter- and wrapper-based feature selection to EEG from 100 participants to distinguish sports from non-sports groups. Genetic Algorithm optimization yielded a minimal feature subset with 93.0 ± 2.7% nested cross-validated accuracy using SVM, and five classifiers showed mean Fleiss' kappa of 0.874 ± 0.051.

papers.title: Nonlinear Feature Modeling Using Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks in Electroencephalography for Depression Classification: Deep Learning Study.
papers.abstract: Depression is a common mental disorder that seriously affects mental health and quality of life. Traditional depression diagnosis mainly relies on clinical interviews and subjective assessments, which may lead to variability in diagnostic outcomes. Electroencephalogram (EEG)-based computer-aided diagnosis has emerged as a promising, objective approach for depression recognition. However, effectively modeling the complex nonlinear characteristics of EEG signals remains a major challenge for existing deep learning methods. This study aimed to investigate the applicability of Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (KANs) for EEG-based depression recognition and to evaluate the effectiveness of KAN-based nonlinear modeling frameworks on frequency-domain EEG features. KAN was introduced into EEG-based depression recognition to enhance nonlinear feature representation of brain electrical signals. Two representative KAN-based convolutional architectures, ConvKAN and its efficiency-optimized variant ConvKAN Efficient, were systematically investigated for EEG classification tasks. These architectures incorporated KANLinear layers together with dynamic grid updating, enhanced weight initialization, and regularization strategies to improve nonlinear modeling capability while maintaining computational efficiency. Extensive experiments were conducted on the EDRA dataset, and the proposed framework was compared with conventional convolutional neural network-based methods and traditional machine learning approaches. Model performance was evaluated using accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score metrics. Experimental results demonstrated that the KAN-based frameworks achieved superior EEG classification performance compared with conventional convolutional neural network-based methods and traditional machine learning approaches. Among the evaluated models, ConvKAN Efficient achieved the best overall performance, with accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score all exceeding 94% on the EDRA dataset. The results indicate that KAN-based architectures can effectively capture the complex nonlinear characteristics of EEG signals while preserving high computational efficiency. This study systematically demonstrates the applicability of KAN-based nonlinear modeling frameworks to EEG-based depression recognition. The proposed framework provides a scalable and effective approach for EEG signal analysis and offers valuable technical support for both theoretical research and clinical applications in computer-aided depression recognition.

ai.reason: Introduces a nonlinear modeling architecture evaluated on EEG features; potentially transferable but framed around depression classification rather than sleep or lightweight deployment.
ai.summary: Introduces Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (ConvKAN and ConvKAN Efficient) for EEG-based depression classification on frequency-domain features using the EDRA dataset. ConvKAN Efficient achieved accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score all exceeding 94%, outperforming conventional CNN and traditional machine learning methods.

papers.title: ADHDeepNet: An Explainable Framework for EEG-Based ADHD Detection From Raw Signals.
papers.abstract: Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) is a common brain disorder in children that can persist into adulthood, affecting social, academic, and career life. Early diagnosis is crucial for managing these impacts on patients and the healthcare system but is often labor-intensive and time-consuming. This paper presents a novel method to improve ADHD diagnosis precision and timeliness by leveraging Deep Learning (DL) approaches and electroencephalogram (EEG) signals. We introduce ADHDeepNet, a deep learning model that utilizes comprehensive temporal-spatial characterization, attention modules, and explainability techniques optimized for EEG signals. ADHDeepNet integrates feature extraction and refinement processes to enhance ADHD diagnosis. The model was trained and validated on a dataset of 121 participants (61 ADHD, 60 Healthy Controls), employing nested cross-validation for robust performance. The proposed two-stage methodology uses a 10-fold cross-subject validation strategy. Initially, each iteration optimizes the model's hyper-parameters with inner 2-fold cross-validation. Then, Additive Gaussian Noise (AGN) with various standard deviations and magnification levels is applied for data augmentation. ADHDeepNet achieved 100% sensitivity and 99.17% accuracy in classifying ADHD/HC subjects. To clarify model explainability and identify key brain regions and frequency bands for ADHD diagnosis, we analyzed the learned weights and activation patterns of the model's primary layers. Additionally, t-distributed Stochastic Neighbor Embedding (t-SNE) visualized high-dimensional data, aiding in interpreting the model's decisions. This study highlights the potential of deep learning and EEG in enhancing ADHD diagnosis accuracy and efficiency.

papers.title: Amplitude-integrated electroencephalogram (aEEG): A bedside window into newborn brain function in the NICU.
papers.abstract: Amplitude-integrated electroencephalography (aEEG) remains an important tool for bedside neonatal brain monitoring. The rapid application of aEEG offers critical practical advantages for bedside clinicians assessing infants at risk for brain injury. aEEG has a distinct clinical niche in evaluations for hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy (HIE) and as a first-line tool for seizure detection, alongside conventional video electroencephalogram (cEEG). Ultimately, the integration of aEEG with a broader multimodal neuromonitoring framework enhances neurodevelopmental prognostication and facilitates individualized bedside interventions, solidifying its relevance in contemporary neonatal neurocritical care.

ai.reason: Amplitude-integrated EEG is a clinically focused neonatal monitoring method; adjacent to EEG analysis but not aimed at sleep staging or computational methods transferable to animal work.
ai.summary: This review describes amplitude-integrated EEG (aEEG) as a bedside tool for neonatal brain monitoring in the NICU, emphasizing its role in hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy evaluation and first-line seizure detection alongside conventional video EEG. It argues that integrating aEEG into multimodal neuromonitoring improves neurodevelopmental prognostication and individualized bedside intervention.

papers.title: Combined eye tracking and electroencephalography during referential selection in dyadic interaction.
papers.abstract: Understanding language in real-world interaction requires methods that integrate auditory, visual, and neural signals. We present a proof-of-concept study combining mobile electroencephalography (EEG) and eye tracking to investigate referential selection during dyadic communication. Using a simplified version of the director task, pairs of participants engaged in naturalistic object-movement instructions while EEG and gaze data were recorded and synchronized via LabStreamingLayer, allowing us to calculate overlap-corrected, regression-based event-related potentials (rERPs) time-locked to spoken nouns and to participants' fixations, focusing on the N400/P300 (300-500 ms) and later (500-800 ms) time windows. Our results show that gaze behavior and fixation-related potentials provide crucial information for interpreting language-related ERPs: Targets competing with occluded referents elicited a stronger posterior positivity consistent with greater attentional demands. Fixation timing systematically modulated neural responses. Contrary to predictions, competitors received little visual attention, indicating that participants prioritized task-relevant information. These findings highlight the potential of multimodal data integration for understanding attentional and predictive mechanisms in real-world communication. Importantly, we show that established analytic techniques, such as artifact subspace reconstruction, independent component analysis, and linear deconvolution for ERP calculation, apply to noisy, naturalistic datasets. In addition, we provide a subsampling sensitivity approach to test the stability of the effects across different sample sizes. This study provides a methodological framework linking gaze and neural activity during interactive language processing. All preprocessing and analysis scripts, along with example datasets, are openly available on OSF ( https://osf.io/5ds4z ; a modified and optimized Python implementation is also available on GitHub: https://github.com/XlinCLab/DGAME ).

papers.title: Aperiodic neural activity predicts cortical excitability in TMS-EEG
papers.abstract: Background: Fluctuating cortical excitability states are inherent to and critical for brain function. They can be probed non-invasively using transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) combined with electroencephalography (EEG) by measuring early local TMS-evoked potentials (EL-TEPs). Pre-stimulus periodic neural activity can predict fluctuating excitability states. To what extent aperiodic neural activity represents a marker of cortical excitability has not been explored. Objectives: We investigated the relationship between pre-stimulus aperiodic and periodic neural activity and EL-TEP amplitude in both the primary motor cortex (M1) and dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC). Methods: Single-pulse TMS was delivered to the left M1 or left DLPFC in 29 and 11 healthy adults, respectively, while EEG was recorded simultaneously. Pre-stimulus EEG was parameterized into aperiodic and periodic components to extract the aperiodic exponent (slope of 1/f-like activity), alpha power (8-13 Hz), and beta power (13-30 Hz). EL-TEP peak-to-peak amplitudes were extracted from approximately 20-65 ms after the TMS pulse. Results: Aperiodic exponent showed a strong negative relationship with EL-TEP amplitude in both M1 and DLPFC, with steeper 1/f-like slopes associated with smaller EL-TEP amplitudes. Inconsistent relationships were found between alpha and beta power with EL-TEP amplitude across the two regions. Conclusions: These findings indicate that pre-stimulus aperiodic neural activity influences cortical excitability in both motor and prefrontal areas. Notably, the aperiodic exponent exhibited stronger associations with cortical excitability compared to periodic alpha or beta power. Brain-state-dependent protocols may benefit from real-time extraction of aperiodic exponent as a target feature to improve the precision and efficacy of TMS.

papers.title: A spatio-temporal attention convolutional network with topology-preserving channel embedding and transformer for EEG decoding.
papers.abstract: EEG-based BCI has shown promising applications in motor rehabilitation and emotion recognition. Given the non-stationarity and variability of EEG signals, it is essential to develop classification models that can effectively extract spatio-temporal features while maintaining strong generalization capabilities. This paper proposes a spatio-temporal attention convolutional network for EEG decoding (E-STACNet) to encode the topological features and temporal characteristics of EEG signals within a unified network framework. It consists of channel-attention (CA) block, convolutional (CV) layers, multi-head self-attention (MSA) and classifier layer. Specifically, CA block encodes spatial topological feature via a topology-preserving channel embedding method. Then convolutional layers are employed to encode low-level temporal information and further extract spatial features, followed by MSA block to highlight the most important temporal information of EEG signals. Finally, the outputs are obtained through two fully-connected layers. We conducted experiments on three public EEG-based datasets including BCI Competition IV dataset 2a, Giga DB and DEAP. The results demonstrate E-STACNet achieves average accuracies of 88.00% and 80.62% on datasets 2a and Giga DB, respectively. On the DEAP, it reaches average accuracies of 96.49% and 96.46% for valence and arousal. The proposed model outperforms other state-of-the-art models on all three datasets. Additionally, the ablation study reveals the importance of topology-preserving channel embedding for the proposed network. Visualization analysis shows E-STACNet could obtain the importance of channels at different locations through the channel-attention mechanism, which demonstrates the interpretability of the proposed model. Overall, the accurate and generalization capabilities of E-STACNet will promote the development of EEG-based BCIs.

papers.title: EEG Resting-State Beta Band Dynamic Functional Connectivity Reveals State-Dependent Disruption of Language Network Lateralisation in First-Episode Schizophrenia.
papers.abstract: Language disorganisation is a core feature of schizophrenia with significant functional consequences. However, its neurophysiological substrates remain poorly characterised, particularly in the early stages of the illness. This study investigated whether first-episode schizophrenia (FES) is associated with disruption in the organisation of language-network lateralisation, using both static and dynamic functional connectivity metrics in the EEG beta band. Thirty-one FES patients and 32 age-matched healthy volunteer subjects (HVS) underwent resting-state 64-channel EEG. Source-level connectivity was estimated using the weighted phase lag index with sliding windows, yielding 979 connectivity matrices per participant. Brain network states (BNS) were identified via k-means clustering. Static connectivity was obtained by time-averaging. Temporal features, graph-theoretical metrics, and language-network laterality indices were extracted for both whole-network and language-specific analyses. Group comparisons used permutation-based tests with family-wise error correction. Static connectivity yielded no significant group differences in any metric. Dynamic analysis identified six BNS. FES showed a significant increase in the variability of the temporal dynamics and graph-theory features of BNS5, a state characterised by parieto-occipital dominance. The core language network laterality index was significantly reduced in FES within BNS1, a state characterised by auditory-visual dominance. BNS1 occurrence correlated negatively with language disorganisation scores. Dynamic BNS-specific language network metrics correlated with verbal fluency performance exclusively in FES. These findings demonstrate that language dysfunction in early psychosis is expressed as state-dependent disruption of brain network stability and language lateralisation, detectable only through dynamic connectivity analysis.

papers.title: [Spectral-topographic features of EEG in patients with varying rates of alcohol dependence progression].
papers.abstract: To compare the spectral-topographic characteristics of the background electroencephalogram (EEG) in patients with alcohol dependence, differing in disease progression rate, as part of a pilot study. A total of 40 male patients with a confirmed diagnosis of alcohol dependence (F10.2 according to ICD-10) were examined. Utilizing a retrospective evaluation of the development of alcohol withdrawal syndrome (AWS), participants were classified into two distinct groups: those exhibiting rapid progression (≤3 years, n=23) and those with slow progression (≥12 years, n=17). Background EEG recordings were obtained using a 16-channel system (10-20 configuration), followed by spectral analysis of absolute power in the theta, alpha-1, alpha-2, beta-1, and beta-2 frequency bands. The analysis revealed that patients with rapid progression demonstrated a statistically significant reduction in the spectral power of the alpha-1 rhythm across all cortical regions (p<0.002 after correction), with the most pronounced effects observed in frontal and central leads. There were also reductions noted in the power of alpha-2, theta (except the parietal region), and beta-1 (limited to the frontal area) frequency bands. Notably, 74% of patients with rapid progression exhibited a low-amplitude («flattened») EEG pattern, whereas 71% in the slow progression group maintained a normal alpha rhythm. The results indicate the presence of a distinct neurophysiological endophenotype associated with the rapid progression of alcohol dependence. Key characteristics of this endophenotype include a overall decrease in the power of the alpha-1 rhythm, particularly in the front-central leads; a decline in theta power (excluding the parietal region); a frontal-specific reduction in beta-1 power; and a significant prevalence of low-amplitude EEG patterns.

papers.title: Quantitative Analysis of Electroencephalography in Hypnosis: A Neurophysiological Approach.
papers.abstract: Hypnosis is a unique state of consciousness marked by heightened response to suggestions, focused attention, and altered cognitive control. This article explores the neural connections involved in hypnosis through electroencephalography (EEG) studies, examining brain changes during hypnosis and their relationship to hypnotic depth and susceptibility. Theta waves, linked to hypnotic depth, are stronger in highly hypnotizable individuals, while gamma waves are associated with focus, suggestion acceptance, and emotional responses. Hypnosis also induces frequency-dependent reorganization of large-scale brain connectivity, particularly in frontal-parietal and attentional networks, enhancing subjective experiences and responsiveness. EEG patterns reveal more dynamic neural activity during hypnosis, which cannot be captured by linear metrics alone. Hemispheric analysis shows greater left-hemisphere activity in highly hypnotizable individuals, particularly in emotionally and verbally mediated tasks, challenging the right-hemisphere dominance model. Event related potential (ERP) findings show that hypnosis affects information processing at both pre-attentional and cognitive levels. These insights contribute to understanding hypnosis' impact on the brain and its potential for personalized therapeutic interventions.

papers.title: Cross-Modal Masked Connectome Transformer for multimodal EEG-fMRI learning in ADHD diagnosis.
papers.abstract: Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) is associated with distributed alterations in large-scale brain systems, making reliable diagnosis from neuroimaging data challenging. EEG-derived and fMRI-derived static functional-connectivity profiles summarize patterns of electrophysiological coupling and hemodynamic covariation, respectively, but their heterogeneous signal mechanisms make direct multimodal alignment difficult. We propose a Cross-Modal Masked Connectome Transformer (CM-MCT) for EEG-fMRI based ADHD diagnosis. Instead of imposing direct correspondence between individual connections, CM-MCT treats each Desikan-Killiany 68-region cortical atlas (DK-68) region of interest (ROI) as a connectivity-profile token and learns to recover masked ROI-level connectome information within and across modalities. The model contains modality-specific Transformer encoders, cross-modal masked connectome objectives, and a bidirectional cross-attention fusion module for diagnostic prediction. Cross-fitted mask perturbations are used to characterize ROI-level model dependence, with explicit assessment of associations with nodal strength and perturbation magnitude. Experiments using repeated five-by-five stratified evaluation of 210 paired HBN subjects demonstrate that the proposed method achieves 89.7% accuracy (95% confidence interval: 85.7%-93.3%) and 94.3% AUC (95% confidence interval: 91.5%-96.8%). Compared with the evaluated methods under matched splits, preprocessing, validation, and model-selection rules, CM-MCT shows the highest mean performance, although the AUC difference from the strongest baseline does not reach statistical significance after multiplicity correction. CM-MCT supports multimodal learning from the complementary network-level information provided by static EEG and fMRI connectivity profiles. Perturbation analysis yields modality-specific ROI sensitivity patterns that are modestly associated with the assessed factors. These heatmaps characterize model dependence without establishing causal involvement or identifying ADHD biomarkers.

papers.title: Supramodal Coding of Detection and Confidence in the Human Cortex
papers.abstract: Perception is inherently multisensory, yet it remains unclear whether the brain detects stimuli and evaluates confidence in these detections using circuits shared across senses or circuits specific to each modality. Prior evidence is limited: scalp electrophysiology cannot localize where a shared code operates, whereas functional imaging cannot resolve its timing. We recorded intracranial activity (stereoelectroencephalography) in eight patients with epilepsy who performed a near-threshold audiovisual detection task in which they reported, on each trial, whether a visual, auditory, or audiovisual stimulus was present and rated their confidence, both overall and separately for each modality. Analyzing high-gamma activity at the single-channel and region-of-interest levels, we found that stimulus detection involved a broadly distributed, largely supramodal set of cortical regions responding regardless of modality, including the insula, dorsomedial prefrontal cortex, and superior temporal gyrus. Multivariate decoders trained to distinguish detected from undetected stimuli in one modality generalized to the other modality, indicating a shared detection code within these regions. Confidence relied on a more mixed architecture but was also substantially supramodal. Finally, the auditory cortex encoded confidence information about its non-preferred (visual) modality, with a similar effect in the visual cortex for auditory confidence, suggesting that the involvement of sensory cortices in confidence is not confined to its preferred input.

papers.title: Variable task difficulty with augmented sensory feedback for motor training in virtual reality.
papers.abstract: This study examined how motor task difficulty and augmented sensory feedback (ASF) modality influence task performance, physiological responses, and perceptual experience during virtual reality (VR)-based upper-limb motor training. Building on related brace- and VR-based ASF platforms previously examined in neurotypical and spinal cord injury cohorts, the long-term goal is to support neurorehabilitation-oriented adaptive VR training; however, the present study used neurotypical participants as an initial validation step. Fourteen right-handed neurotypical participants used a supportive upper-limb brace and surface electromyography (EMG) for myoelectric control of a virtual robotic arm in a two-dimensional tracking task. A 2 × 2 within-subject design crossed ASF modality (visual feedback versus visual + haptic feedback) with task difficulty (straight-line versus sinusoidal trajectory). Outcomes included normalized path length, task completion time, movement jerk, alpha- and beta-band electroencephalogram (EEG) power over motor cortex, heart rate, EMG amplitude, EMG-displacement-based virtual work, and perceptual ratings of agency, motivation, and utility. Short-term pre-to-post percentage changes were computed for each measure. VHF straight-line training produced the largest reductions in normalized path length (-4.69%) and completion time (-6.12%), whereas VHF sinusoid training produced the largest reductions in movement jerk (-5.67%) and virtual work (-13.33%). ASF modality affected path length, completion time, jerk, EMG amplitude, and virtual work, whereas task difficulty modulated beta-band EEG power and the physiological index. Changes in path length were positively associated with changes in completion time and EMG amplitude. These findings suggest that ASF modality and task difficulty can differentially shape short-term behavioral, physiological, and perceptual responses in healthy participants. The exploratory distribution of participant-specific best-case conditions motivates future studies using independent trial subsets to evaluate whether behavioral and physiological measures can support individualized VR training.

papers.title: Late Integration of Prior Expectations During Precision-Weighted Perceptual Decisions.
papers.abstract: Adaptive perceptual decision-making relies on the ability to combine sensory evidence with prior expectations in a precision-weighted manner. Although Bayesian inference provides a clear normative account of how such integration should occur, the neural mechanisms through which the brain represents and combines priors and likelihoods remain poorly understood. Across two preregistered experiments, we investigated how the precision of learned priors and sensory likelihoods influence visual motion judgements and associated neural activity patterns during a random-dot motion estimation task. Neurotypical adult participants (N=80, 58 female) reported directions of visual motion stimuli, with motion coherence varying randomly across trials. Prior expectations over the continuous motion direction space were manipulated block-wise by implicitly varying the probabilities with which different motion directions were presented. Consistent with precision-weighted inference, response accuracy improved as motion coherence increased with robust response biases toward the expected motion direction. Neural activity measured using electroencephalography (EEG) revealed reliable effects of prior expectation on the univariate central-parietal positivity (CPP), consistent with reduced accumulation of sensory evidence under informative priors. Multivariate analysis using inverted-encoding models revealed robust effects of prior precision on stimulus-specific neural representations, but only late, during response planning stages. Together, these findings suggest that priors learned over a continuous space do not modulate the encoding of sensory evidence and are instead integrated later in the decision-process.Significance Statement Perceptual decisions require combining noisy sensory input with prior expectations about what is likely to occur. It remains unclear how the brain integrates prior expectations with incoming sensory evidence. Using a visual motion task and concurrent brain imaging, we show that expectations do not alter early stimulus-encoding, but are instead integrated at later stages of decision formation and action planning. These findings add nuance to influential theories proposing that learned expectations directly affect stimulus representations and instead highlight their contribution to later decision-related processes. This work advances understanding of how the brain uses experience to optimise perceptual decisions under uncertainty.

papers.title: Responses to unannounced rule changes in adults with developmental disabilities: A community-based pilot study with consumer-grade EEG

We recruited adults with developmental disabilities, including those with intellectual disability, at a community day-service center. We administered a probabilistic reversal learning task and recorded resting-state electroencephalography (EEG) via a 14-channel wireless EEG system. Among the 12 adults who performed the task, total errors were comparable across participants (range 31-57), whereas a switch bias index, contrasting perseverative errors (persisting with the previously correct option) with regressive errors (failing to maintain the newly correct option), ranged from -0.96 to +0.91. In the 9 participants included in resting-state EEG analyses, a flatter aperiodic spectrum over the frontal cluster (preregistered, but selected as the focus post hoc) was associated with fewer switches after negative feedback ({rho} = .80) and more perseverative errors ({rho} = -.72). The preregistered parieto-occipital cluster showed the same direction ({rho} = .69, 95% confidence interval [-.11, .97], n = 8), which was opposite to the preregistered prediction. Frontal alpha peak amplitude was associated with accuracy ({rho} = .77), and the between-run reliability of resting-state measures was .82-.99. These findings provide preliminary evidence that EEG recorded in community settings can capture individual differences in how people respond to change. Field measurement that includes people with intellectual disability may help extend the evidence base for the Sustainable Development Goals of good health and well-being (SDG 3) and reduced inequalities (SDG 10).

papers.title: Spectral power and functional connectivity of resting EEG in people exposed to armed conflict and controls
papers.abstract: Exposure to armed conflict can leave persistent effects on mental health, yet its neurophysiological correlates remain poorly characterized, particularly in populations exposed to prolonged violence outside narrowly defined post traumatic stress disorder samples. Eyes closed EEG was analysed for 240 seconds per participant. We quantified absolute and relative spectral power across delta, theta, alpha and beta bands and regional functional connectivity using weighted phase lag index in theta, alpha and beta. Group comparisons were adjusted for age, education, sex and assessment year, with correction across 78 EEG contrasts. Median occipital and global alpha power was lower in exposed participants, although adjusted estimates were close to the null and confidence intervals were broad. Temporal theta relative power was lower in exposed participants at nominal significance, but this association did not survive Holm correction. No spectral power or regional connectivity contrast remained significant after multiple testing correction. Exploratory associations between EEG measures and MoCA performance were modest in participants with confirmed scores. These findings provide a systematic characterization of resting EEG after exposure to armed conflict in a population shaped by prolonged violence and displacement. They also indicate that large or widespread alterations in resting spectral power and connectivity were not detectable with the current sample and analytical framework, while defining candidate signals and methodological priorities for larger studies of conflict related brain health.

The comparison group consisted of 30 children with combined ADHD (ADHD-C), also aged 12 to 14 years. The control group comprised 30 children in the same age range without any neuropsychiatric disorders. The study used several methods, including S. Lee's SCT scale for assessing the severity of SCT symptoms, the Multidimensional Fatigue Inventory (MFI-20), the Daytime Sleepiness Scale, and T.A. Fotekova and T.V. Cortexin was administered intramuscularly at a standard dosage of 10 mg every other day across 10 injections to patients diagnosed with SCT. papers.title: Selection vs. integration task demands shape the similarity of information neural coding
papers.abstract: Attention is a function that enables selection and integration of multiple sources of information. However, how these demands influence neural coding of information is not well understood. In this study we used EEG to examine how the selection vs. integration of stimuli shapes the content and geometry reflected on neural patterns, during both preparation and target processing. Participants performed a size judgement task in a cue-target paradigm that, depending on the block, required judging either the size of a selected item and ignoring the additional stimulus or integrating both to respond. Decoding analyses showed that under selection demands, categorical templates of the cued stimulus were active during preparation and target coding, contrasting with integration, where patterns linked to the cued category could be observed only during preparation. Notably, RSA suggested specific exemplar encoding during its processing, which was sustained also across the post-stimulus window during selection, yet was not observable under integration contexts. Our results also suggest that attentional demands shape the similarity between stimulus categories by increasing the distance between selected stimuli and distractors or by reducing it between to-be-integrated information. Overall, this study uncovers the dynamics of stimulus encoding under selection and integration demands, offering crucial advances to understand how top-down processes shape information representation in the human brain.

papers.title: Effects of EEG neurofeedback in adults with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder: a systematic review of randomised and non-randomised studies.
papers.abstract: Pharmacotherapy is recommended as the first-line treatment for adult attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), yet some individuals show partial or inadequate response associated with adverse effects. These limitations have prompted interest in adjunctive or alternative interventions. Electroencephalography (EEG) neurofeedback is a non-pharmacological intervention for ADHD, which enables self-regulation of neural activity. This systematic review synthesised clinical, cognitive, and electrophysiological outcomes of EEG neurofeedback in adult ADHD, and examined standard versus personalised training protocols. Following PRISMA guidelines, four databases (PubMed, ScienceDirect, Ovid, Web of Science) were searched from 1960 to October 2025 for this PROSPERO-registered review (ID: CRD420251020898). Eligible studies included adults (≥ 18 years) with a formal ADHD diagnosis undergoing EEG neurofeedback. Outcomes comprised symptom severity, cognitive performance, electrophysiology, and adverse events. Risk of bias was assessed using RoB 2 and ROBINS-I V2. Seven studies (three RCTs, four non-randomised; n = 390) met inclusion criteria. Protocols included theta/beta (n = 1), slow cortical potential (n = 1), alpha downregulation training (n = 1) and personalised approaches guided by individual alpha peak frequency (n = 3) or QEEG profiles (n = 1). Naturalistic and personalised studies reported large symptom reductions, whereas RCTs revealed small, generally non-significant effects relative to controls. Cognitive improvements were inconsistently reported and largely attributable to practice effects. Electrophysiological changes were protocol-specific without convergence across studies. No treatment-related adverse events were observed. Evidence remains limited by methodological heterogeneity, small samples, variable controls, inconsistent learning metrics, and risk of bias. Current RCTs do not demonstrate evidence of efficacy over placebo. Blinded, adequately powered trials using standardised learning measures are needed to clarify mechanisms of neurofeedback.

papers.title: Functional and Organic Pseudo-Orthostatic Tremor: Clinical Features, Electrophysiology, and Treatment Outcomes in a Retrospective Cohort

It is believed to be secondary to other neurological disorders in a large proportion of cases. Surface electromyography (sEMG) can identify its core characteristics and differentiate it from other similar disorders such as primary orthostatic tremor (POT) and orthostatic myoclonus (OM). Data on demographics, clinical characteristics, sEMG findings, pharmacological treatments, ancillary investigations and patient reported outcomes were collected. Among the 29 patients with organic psOT, 21 (72.4%) fulfilled the diagnostic criteria for essential tremor (ET), while an identifiable neurological cause was established in four (13.8%). sEMG findings differed between functional and organic psOT, with the latter often displaying features consistent with weight-bearing hyperkinesias. Conclusions: Our retrospective study suggests that psOT is most often associated with ET, while an identifiable neurological cause was found in a relatively small proportion of patients. We also describe functional psOT as a previously unrecognized clinical presentation of FND.

papers.title: Is Less More? Exploring the Visual Processes of Minimalist and Complex Photography Through Eye Tracking and EEG.
papers.abstract: In a world filled with an overwhelming amount of visual information, the clean and distinctive visual style of minimalist photography stands out. However, empirical research on how minimalist style affects visual cognition and psychological responses remains limited. The present study investigated the effects of photographic style (minimalist versus complex) on viewers' visual behavior, emotional responses, and brainwave state by conducting quantitative psychological experiments. Thirty participants viewed photographs in one of the two styles. Eye-tracking, consumer-grade electroencephalography (EEG), and subjective psychological assessment data were collected, enabling comprehensive evaluation of how the participants looked at, responded to, and emotionally engaged with the images. At the level of visual behavior, minimalism elicited significantly reduced number of fixations and saccades, but the duration of a single fixation is significantly longer, and the heatmap hotspots are highly concentrated, presenting a focused processing pattern of fewer but longer gazes. On a psychological level, minimalism evoked significantly less feeling of complexity and greater relaxation, although there was no significant difference in the aesthetics score between the two styles. In terms of brainwave state, viewing minimalist images resulted in significantly higher attention eSense levels, while the meditation eSense level did not show a significant difference. The results of this study therefore show that minimalist composition may influence the visual search pattern to be more focused, which is compatible with the tendency of simplified organization predicted by the principle of simplification. This study not only deepens the theoretical understanding of the psychological mechanisms of minimalist aesthetics, but also provides practical reference for visual communication and image creation of minimalist composition serving as an effective strategy for guiding the eyes toward the core subject.

papers.title: Neural Response to Monetary and Social Feedback in Childhood: Processing Reward and Loss in Relation to Peer Outcomes and Anxiety Symptoms.
papers.abstract: Anxiety disorders are the most prevalent psychiatric conditions in childhood and are associated with social functioning impairment. How youth process rewards may contribute to the development of social impairment in childhood anxiety. Although aberrant reward processing is a well-established mechanism of psychopathology, associations with anxiety remain inconsistent and limited, especially in childhood. This study investigated neural response to monetary and social reward feedback in relation to anxiety and peer functioning in children. Children (N=106; Age=8.12±.68 years) completed the Doors Task and the Island Getaway Task while electroencephalogram (EEG) recordings assessed event-related potentials (ERPs) to wins and losses. Parents completed questionnaires assessing child anxiety, depression, and peer relations. Contrary to pre-registered hypotheses, we found a significant Valence (reward versus loss) by Condition (monetary versus social) interaction. Specifically, children exhibited greater neural response to monetary loss than reward, but showed the opposite pattern in the social condition, with greater neural response to social reward than loss. Higher child- and parent-reported total and generalized anxiety predicted significantly greater neural response to monetary reward, but not monetary loss or social feedback. As hypothesized, anxiety symptoms significantly moderated the association between neural response and peer relations, demonstrating that for highly anxious children, a greater neural response to social loss predicted worse peer relations. Findings demonstrate differences in neural response to monetary and social feedback processing. Moreover, the distinct vulnerability to social rejection might impair peer functioning in anxious children, suggesting that clinical interventions targeting social rejection processing may effectively improve peer outcomes in childhood anxiety.

papers.title: EEG signature in psychiatrist's subjective experience: a pilot study.
papers.abstract: The Assessment of Clinician's Subjective Experience (ACSE) is a self-report questionnaire developed to evaluate clinicians' subjective experiences during patient interactions. While its psychometric properties and clinical validity have been supported, its neurobiological correlates have not yet been investigated. In this pilot study, two clinicians and ten patients participated in a three-phase protocol comprising: (1) a first clinical interview, (2) ACSE administration, and (3) listening to the audio recording of the first clinical interview. EEG activity was recorded from clinicians during both the first clinical interview and questionnaire administration. Neural data were analyzed in terms of relative power spectral density, node strength, and global efficiency computed from imaginary coherence. Clinicians were psychiatrists, one male and one female. Seven patients were diagnosed with mixed anxiety and depressive disorder, and three with unspecified anxiety disorders. ACSE scores were highest for the Difficulty in attunement and Engagement dimensions, consistent with previous literature. EEG findings revealed dimension-specific and topographically distinct oscillatory patterns for only two ACSE dimensions: Difficulty in Attunement and Engagement. More limited evidence emerged for Disconfirmation. Functional connectivity analyses indicated different network profiles, characterized by differences in global efficiency patterns. Correlational analyses further identified significant associations between ACSE dimensions and EEG-derived features. These preliminary findings provide initial evidence that clinicians' subjective experiences during clinical encounters could be associated with measurable neural signatures, offering a novel perspective on the neurobiological basis of intersubjective processes in clinical settings.

papers.title: The effect of text-picture consistency on memory integration in college students: Evidence from ERPs.
papers.abstract: In multimedia learning, individuals often need to integrate textual and visual information. The neural mechanisms underlying how consistency between text and pictures affects memory integration remain unclear. To examine the effect of text-picture consistency on memory integration in college students and to determine the processing time at which this effect occurs. Totally 28 Chinese college students (nfemale = 20, nmale = 8; Mage = 21.64 ± 2.30) participated in this experiment. An adapted pictorial demonstration paradigm was employed. Participants sequentially learned two pairs of text-picture stem facts (consistent vs. inconsistent), separated by an interval, followed by a recognition test for stem and integrated facts. Behavioural and event-related potential (ERP) data were recorded simultaneously. Under the text-picture consistency condition, college students showed significantly better memory integration performance than under the inconsistency condition (58% vs. 48%). EEG results showed that the text-picture inconsistency condition (i.e., the picture and text within a single stem fact were semantically mismatched) elicited a larger P600 wave (500-800 ms) than the text-picture consistency condition, suggesting that text-picture inconsistency primarily induces conflict and integration difficulties during late cognitive processing. No significant differences were observed in the early N400 component. Text-picture consistency facilitates memory integration primarily during late processing, aligning with cognitive theories of multimedia learning. Educationally, it serves as a key quality indicator for multimedia material design. Instructors should prioritize semantic alignment and assess knowledge integration during evaluation.

papers.title: Early neurocognitive outcomes following SEEG with radiofrequency thermocoagulation.
papers.abstract: Characterization of early neuropsychological outcomes following SEEG with radiofrequency thermocoagulation (RFTHC) is essential to guide patient expectations around return to work, study, and caregiving. The current study aimed to describe the early neurocognitive sequelae of SEEG. Consecutive patients undergoing SEEG were prospectively recruited from two tertiary epilepsy centers in Melbourne, Australia. Patients were administered the Repeatable Battery for the Assessment of Neuropsychological Status (RBANS) via telehealth before and 3 weeks after SEEG (M = 19.69 days, SD = 4.41). Given the telehealth platform, the coding subtest was substituted for the Symbol Digit Modalities Test, and a modified score of global cognitive function was calculated. To evaluate group changes, paired sample t-tests were performed. Reliable change indices were computed to explore individual-level changes. Pearson's correlation coefficients evaluated relationships between change in global cognitive function and SEEG admission variables. SEEG patients were invited to complete a semi-structured interview canvassing the recovery following SEEG. Twenty-eight patients completed the neuropsychological examination (M = 37.89 years, SD = 9.72, range = 17-56 years, 54% female). All patients underwent RFTHC with a mean of 11.43 (SD = 6.87, range = 2-28) coagulation sites. At a whole group level, 3-weeks post SEEG there was no evidence for global nor domain-specific cognitive change. Reliable change indices with 90% confidence revealed only 4% (1/28) declined on at least two measures and 10% (3/28) showed psychometric improvement. Pearson's correlational coefficients showed no evidence for association between change in global cognitive function with SEEG factors including admission length, number of spontaneous or stimulated seizures, number of electrodes, or number of RFTHC sites. Subjective reports of language change tended to be accompanied by a decline on the RBANS language index that did not meet reliable change criteria. Most patients reported returning to work around 4 weeks post SEEG. By 3 weeks, gross cognitive functioning tends to be in keeping with pre-SEEG performances for most patients. These findings have direct clinical implications for SEEG neuropsychological counseling. SEEG is increasingly used to guide epilepsy surgery. Despite this, little is known about the cognitive recovery in the weeks following the procedure. We found that for most patients, broad cognitive functioning 3 weeks after SEEG with coagulation was consistent with function before SEEG, with only a small minority showing significant changes. Some people who reported language difficulties also showed a decline on language testing, although this was often small. Of those patients working before SEEG, most returned to work by 4 weeks. These results provide important evidence to guide patient counseling, recovery planning, and management after SEEG.

papers.title: Mapping the Research Landscape and Global Trends: A Bibliometric Analysis of Event-related Potential in Alzheimer's Disease.
papers.abstract: There is an urgent need for objective biomarkers to facilitate early diagnosis and dynamic monitoring of Alzheimer's Disease (AD). Event-Related Potential (ERP), as a neuroelectrophysiological technique with high temporal resolution, shows great promise in addressing this demand. However, the macro-level developmental trajectory, research status, and frontier directions within this field remain to be systematically elucidated. This study employs bibliometric methods to delineate the development trends, knowledge structures, and research frontiers of ERP applications in AD, thereby offering a novel perspective for early diagnosis, dynamic monitoring, and efficacy assessment. Publications related to ERP and AD were retrieved and screened from the Web of Science Core Collection. A comprehensive quantitative and visual analysis was conducted using Microsoft Excel, CiteSpace, VOSviewer, and the bibliometrix package in R. The analysis covered publication trends, national/institutional collaboration networks, author co-occurrence, core journals, reference and keyword co-occurrence, and clustering. The number of annual publications in this field continued to grow. The United States, China, and Italy were the most productive countries, whereas the cooperation network among institutions and authors was decentralized. Keyword clustering identified six major research topics: P300/N200, Mismatch Negativity (MMN), N170, N400, Olfactory Event-Related Potential (OERP), and Electroencephalography (EEG). An analysis of the global research landscape reveals that ERP research has developed from an exploratory tool in the field of AD to an active research field of neuroscience. Journal and citation analysis indicate that the field has distinct clinical problem-driven features; keyword cluster analysis revealed six major themes corresponding to classical cognitive assessment, early sensory memory, and social cognition. Thematic analysis revealed that MMN and other ERP components that are sensitive to early abnormalities may become future research hotspots; however, the overall cooperation in this field still shows a certain degree of geographical concentration and institutional dispersion. In the future, it is necessary to build a closer international and interdisciplinary cooperation network, establish a standardized ERP evaluation scheme, and embed it throughout the entire process of early identification, staging, and monitoring of the effect of intervention in AD. This research systematically presents the current state of research, hotspots, and evolutionary trends in ERP in the field of AD. The results suggest that in the future, a closer international and interdisciplinary cooperation network and further prospective clinical validation are needed to clarify the diagnostic performance and practical application value of ERP, thereby promoting its clinical application.

papers.title: Vibrational dynamics of TODD-graphene nanosheets via molecular dynamics simulations and machine-learning surrogate models: implications for adaptive nanomechanical devices.
papers.abstract: TODD-Graphene (TODD-G), a porous two-dimensional carbon allotrope composed of interconnected 3-8-10-12 carbon rings, has recently emerged as a promising candidate for nanoelectromechanical and adaptive nanodevice applications due to its metallic conductivity, mechanical compliance, and topologically engineered phonon structure. In this work, the vibrational dynamics of TODD-G nanosheets were systematically investigated to establish structure-property relationships governing resonant behavior under varying geometric, thermal, mechanical, and defect conditions. Fundamental frequencies were found to span 2.93-13.28 THz and follow the classical f ∝ L - 2 scaling relation. Increasing temperature from 1 to 1000 K reduced resonance frequencies by up to 22% because of thermal expansion and anharmonic phonon interactions, while tensile strain up to 10% enhanced frequencies by more than 50%, yielding gauge factors of 5.3-5.7 that exceed those of graphene. Vacancy defects significantly degraded quality factors and resonance stability, whereas multilayer stacking improved energy retention despite modest frequency reduction. Boundary conditions strongly altered modal spectra, with clamped-clamped configurations producing the highest frequencies and quality factors. Phonon density-of-states analysis revealed distinct acoustic, mixed, and optical vibrational regimes with a maximum phonon cutoff frequency of 56.5 THz. To accelerate device-level optimization, machine-learning surrogate models were developed for predicting resonance frequency and quality factor across the multidimensional design space. Gradient-boosting models achieved excellent predictive accuracy ( R 2 = 0.98 for frequency and R 2 = 0.972 for quality factor), demonstrating that thermal activation and vacancy concentration dominate vibrational dissipation mechanisms. The combined molecular dynamics and machine-learning framework establishes TODD-G as a promising platform for tunable nanoresonators, strain sensors, RF filters, vibration energy harvesters, and cryogenic nanomechanical systems. Atomic-scale simulations were performed using classical molecular dynamics within the large-scale atomic/molecular massively parallel simulator (LAMMPS) package. Interatomic interactions were described using the adaptive intermolecular reactive empirical bond order (AIREBO) potential with activated Lennard-Jones and torsional terms, while multilayer van der Waals interactions employed a 12-6 Lennard-Jones potential. Structural relaxation was conducted using conjugate-gradient energy minimization. Thermal equilibration employed the Nosé-Hoover thermostat within the canonical (NVT) ensemble, followed by microcanonical (NVE) simulations for vibrational analysis using a timestep of 0.5 fs. Vibrational properties were extracted using impulse-response analysis, velocity autocorrelation functions, harmonic forcing, fast Fourier transform (FFT) spectral analysis, and phonon density-of-states calculations. Simulations systematically examined the effects of nanosheet size, temperature (1-1000 K), tensile strain (0-10%), vacancy-defect concentration (0.5-5%), multilayer stacking (1-5 layers), and boundary conditions (free-free, clamped-free, simply supported, and clamped-clamped). Machine-learning surrogate models including linear regression, support-vector regression with radial-basis-function kernels, random forest regression, and gradient-boosting regression were trained using an 80/20 train-test split and five-fold cross-validation to predict resonance frequency and quality factor across the multidimensional parameter space.

papers.title: Elucidating the relationship between protein amide I, II, and III bands and secondary structures by localized anharmonic vibrational calculations.
papers.abstract: The amide I, II, and III spectra of the insulin dimer and ubiquitin were investigated using our recently developed localized, second-order vibrational quasi-degenerate perturbation theory (VQDPT2) combined with quantum mechanics/molecular mechanics calculations. By averaging over ten snapshots from molecular dynamics trajectories, we confirmed that the computed spectra converged to a sufficient degree. Although the method has intrinsic limitations due to the neglect of vibrational coupling between neighboring amide groups, we found that the method provides a useful basis for spectral analysis of these proteins. The analysis of the averaged amide I, II, and III bands revealed that, for both proteins, the amide II and III peak positions tend to be closely associated with the coil contribution, whereas the origin of the amide I maximum is more protein dependent. The calculated amide I and III frequencies of the coil structures showed good agreement with experimental values. The spectra of each secondary structure were further subdivided according to the type of hydrogen bonding within the secondary structure. For structurally constrained α-helix and β-sheet structures, hydrogen-bond-dependent amide I frequency shifts were found to correlate with changes in the amide dihedral angles (O=C-N-H). Localized VQDPT2 enables direct interpretation of amide band shifts associated with conformational changes and provides a deeper understanding of the structural origin responsible for these band shifts.
